## Introduction

Associative forward blocking refers to the attenuation of learning about a stimulus-outcome relationship when the stimulus is accompanied by another one that has already been established to reliably predict that outcome [@beesley2011; @paskewitz2020].

Behavioural studies combined with eye-tracking have demonstrated that blocking occurs in human associative learning and that it can be accounted for by learned *in*attention to the blocked cue [@kruschke2005; @beesley2011; @lepelley2007; @wills2007; @luque2018]. Two candidate mechanisms have been proposed to explain this phenomenon: rapid **attentional shifts**, whereby redirecting attention away from the blocked cue improves learning, and **attentional competition**, whereby cues vie for a limited attentional resource [@kruschke2005; @paskewitz2020].

However, no definitive experiment capable of discriminating between these two proposed mechanisms has yet been conducted. Using simulations, @paskewitz2020 derived an experimental design that could, in principle, adjudicate between the two accounts.

The primary aims of this project are to:

1.  replicate the findings of @beesley2011 in a large sample, and
2.  design and implement an extension of this paradigm that allows for direct comparison between the attentional shift and attentional competition accounts of blocking, drawing on the theoretical analysis by @paskewitz2020.

## Forward Blocking

Blocking was first described in rodents by @kamin1969 and later demonstrated in human contingency learning by @dickinson1984 and @shanks1985. The basic phenomenon can be explained by simple associative learning models such as the Rescorla–Wagner model [@rescorla1972]. However, subsequent work suggested that blocking is accompanied by shifts of attention away from blocked cues, and can thus be better explained by attentional theories of associative learning [e.g., @mackintosh1975; @pearce1980].

Although alternative explanations based on propositional reasoning have been proposed ***(cite propositional theories)***, learned attention accounts remain influential and continue to be used in both empirical and computational work [@paskewitz2020; @paskewitz2023; @kelly2025a; @kelly2025b]^[**Look for more broad use of the theories. It is surely there, they are popular.**]. Rather than adjudicating directly between competing theoretical frameworks, the present study focuses on subjecting learned attention models to a severe empirical testing^[**Cite Deborah Mayo here?**].

Evidence for attentional mechanisms in blocking comes from several lines of research, including experimental manipulations of cue competition [@lepelley2007; @beesley2011], eye-tracking studies of overt attention [@kruschke2005; @wills2007; @lepelley2007], behavioural measures of attentional bias [@liu2013; @luque2018], and computational simulations of attentional learning models [@kruschke2005; @paskewitz2020; @paskewitz2023; see also @sewell2012 for discussion]. Building on recent simulation work [@paskewitz2020], the present study designs an experimental procedure aimed at testing key predictions of learned-attention theories about blocking and its relation to attention.

## Experiment 1 (replication)

@tbl-blocking-original shows the experimental design employed by @beesley2011.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-blocking-original
#| tbl-cap: "Associational blocking experimental design as used by @beesley2011"

tibble(
  stage_1_cue = c("A", "C", "E", "G", "I", "L", "O", "R"),
  stage_1_out = rep(c(rep(1, 2), rep(2, 2)), 2),
  stage_2_cue = c("AB", "CD", "EF", "GH", "JK", "MN", "PQ", "ST"),
  stage_2_out = rep(c(rep(1, 2), rep(2, 2)), 2),
  stage_3_cue = c("BK", "DN", "FQ", "HT", rep(NA, 4)),
  stage_3_out = c(rep(3:4, 2), rep(NA, 4)),
  test_cue = c("BT", "DQ", "FN", "HK", "BN", "DK", "FT", "HQ"),
  test_out = "?",
  test_pref = rep(4:3, 4)
) |>
  gt() |>
  #apa_style() |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "") |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 1", columns = starts_with("stage_1")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 2", columns = starts_with("stage_2")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 3", columns = starts_with("stage_3")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Test", columns = starts_with("test")) |>
  cols_label(
    ends_with("cue") ~ "Cues",
    ends_with("out") ~ "Outcome",
    ends_with("pref") ~ "Preferred"
  )
```

## Eperiment 2 (extension)

@tbl-blocking-extension shows the experimental design of @beesley2011 after changes .

```{r}
#| label: tbl-blocking-extension
#| tbl-cap: "Associational blocking experimental design proposed by @paskewitz2020"

tibble(
  stage_1_cue = c("A", "C", "E", "G", "I", "L", "O", "R"),
  stage_1_out = rep(c(rep(1, 2), rep(2, 2)), 2),
  stage_2_cue = c("AB", "CD", "EF", "GH", "JK", "MN", "PQ", "ST"),
  stage_2_out = rep(c(rep(1, 2), rep(2, 2)), 2),
  stage_3_cue = c("BU", "DV", "FW", "HX", rep(NA, 4)),
  stage_3_out = c(rep(3:4, 2), rep(NA, 4)),
  test_cue = c("BX", "DW", "FV", "HU", "BV", "DU", "FX", "HW"),
  test_out = "?",
  test_pred_shift = rep(3:4, 4),
  test_pred_comp = rep(4:3, 4)
) |>
  gt() |>
  #apa_style() |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "") |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 1", columns = starts_with("stage_1")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 2", columns = starts_with("stage_2")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 3", columns = starts_with("stage_3")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Model Predictions", columns = contains("pred")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Test", columns = starts_with("test")) |>
  cols_label(
    ends_with("cue") ~ "Cues",
    ends_with("out") ~ "Outcome",
    ends_with("shift") ~ "Shifting (RSWAC)",
    ends_with("comp") ~ "Competition\n(CompAct)"
  )
```
